Evidence · Federal Rules, Article VIII

The Hearsay Rule

A witness is on the stand, under oath, and repeats something a person said outside the courtroom. Whether the jury may hear it is among the most-tested questions in Evidence — and the answer usually turns on why the statement is offered. This lesson teaches the full analysis: the definition, the not-for-truth purposes, the 801(d) exclusions, the 803 and 804 exceptions, layered statements, and the Confrontation Clause. You practice by ruling on objections, and you finish with a closed-book docket.

“Call my accuser before my face …” — Sir Walter Raleigh, on trial for treason, 1603, as quoted in Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36, 44 (2004)

§1 Why the rule exists §2 The definition §3 Offered for what purpose §4 The 801(d) exclusions §5 The 803 exceptions §6 The 804 exceptions §7 Layers and confrontation §8 The final

First ruling

Rule on this before anything is explained

On the stand · State v. Avery

“Maria told me the delivery truck ran the red light.”

— the witness, testifying at trial. Opposing counsel objects: hearsay.

You are the judge. Is it hearsay?

± Half right. A ruling needs a fact you were never given: what the statement is offered to prove. Maria's words were said out of court — that much you can check. But hearsay has a second requirement: the statement must be offered to prove the truth of what it asserts. If counsel offers it to prove the truck ran the light, sustain the objection. If counsel offers it to prove something else — say, that Maria was conscious and able to speak after the crash — overrule it. The transcript never told you the purpose, so "yes" was a guess.
± Half right. A ruling needs a fact you were never given: what the statement is offered to prove. Maria's words were said out of court — that part is done. But hearsay has a second requirement: the statement must be offered to prove the truth of what it asserts. If counsel offers it to prove the truck ran the light, it is hearsay and you should sustain. If counsel offers it to prove that Maria was conscious and able to speak after the crash, overrule. The transcript never told you the purpose, so "no" was a guess.
✓ Correct. You cannot rule yet, and knowing that is the point. Hearsay has two requirements, and the transcript only answers the first: the statement was made out of court. The second — is it offered to prove the truth of what it asserts? — is missing. Offered to prove the truck ran the light, it is hearsay. Offered to prove Maria was conscious and able to speak after the crash, it is not.
The two questions every hearsay ruling turns on:
1. Was the statement made out of court? — yes, Maria spoke before trial.
2. Is it offered to prove the truth of what it asserts? — the record doesn't say. That question is where this lesson begins.
Next · Why the rule exists ↓

§1 · Why the rule exists

A trial that made a rule

Courts test what witnesses say in a specific way: the witness swears an oath, the jury watches them speak, and the other side cross-examines. Cross-examination probes four weak points in any human report — the witness may have seen it wrong, remembered it wrong, said it in a misleading way, or lied. Lawyers call these the hearsay dangers.

An out-of-court statement skips all of that. The person who actually spoke — the declarant — never takes the oath, the jury never sees them, and no one can cross-examine a sentence. The witness on the stand can only vouch that the words were said, not that they were true.

English law learned what that costs at a famous trial. In 1603, Sir Walter Raleigh was tried for treason. The Crown's case rested on the sworn examination of his alleged accomplice, Lord Cobham — a paper, taken privately, that Cobham had since disavowed. Put yourself in the prosecutor's chair before you read what happened:

You are the Attorney General. Cobham has already recanted once. Call him to testify live, and he may fall apart in front of the jury. The rules of the day let you simply read his sworn examination aloud instead. What do you do?

✗ Not what happened. Attorney General Edward Coke read the paper. Of course he did — the examination could not recant, could not be questioned, and could not lose the case. That is the incentive the rule against hearsay exists to remove: when untested statements are admissible, the rational prosecutor prefers them to live witnesses.
✓ That is what happened. Attorney General Edward Coke read the paper — the examination could not recant, could not be questioned, and could not lose the case. You reasoned like a 1603 prosecutor, which is exactly the incentive the rule against hearsay exists to remove: when untested statements are admissible, the rational prosecutor prefers them to live witnesses.

Raleigh demanded the obvious: “Call my accuser before my face …” The judges refused. He was convicted and eventually executed. The scandal of that trial pushed English law toward two connected ideas: parties should be able to confront the witnesses against them, and statements that cannot be tested by cross-examination should presumptively stay out.

Hold on to the reason, because it organizes everything that follows. The rule excludes out-of-court statements offered for their truth because no one can test them. Every exception you will meet marks a situation where that objection loses force — either the circumstances of the statement substitute for testing, or the declarant can in fact be tested.

The chain, 1603 → 2004

The Crown holds a paper. Cobham's sworn examination accuses Raleigh — taken privately, later disavowed by Cobham himself.
The prosecutor reads it. A paper cannot recant or be cross-examined, so Coke prefers it to the living witness.
The accused objects. Raleigh: “Call my accuser before my face …” The judges refuse. Conviction; later, execution.
The scandal becomes law. English courts develop the right to confront accusers and a rule excluding untested out-of-court statements.
Exceptions grow at the edges. Where circumstances substitute for cross-examination, or the declarant can still be tested, courts let statements in.
The modern echo. The Federal Rules codify the system in 1975. In 2004, Crawford v. Washington cites Raleigh's trial to revive the confrontation right for criminal cases.

Press Watch for the narrated walkthrough.

The four dangers cross-examination tests

Each danger is a way an honest-sounding sentence can be wrong. Cross-examination exists to probe all four — and none of them can be probed when the declarant is absent.

PerceptionDid the declarant see or hear the event accurately in the first place?
MemoryDid the declarant remember it accurately by the time they spoke?
NarrationDid their words say what they meant, or were they ambiguous?
SincerityWere they telling the truth at all?
Next · The definition ↓

§2 · The definition

Three working parts, one at a time

The formal definition of hearsay is one sentence, but it has three parts that each do real work. Meet each part in a scenario before you read the sentence — it will land as a recap instead of a puzzle.

Part one — a “statement” is an intended assertion

Outside the bank

An officer asks the crowd which way the robber went. A bystander says nothing — and points at the alley.

At trial, the officer describes the pointing to prove the robber went down the alley.

No words were spoken. Is the pointing a “statement”?

✓ Correct. The bystander meant the point as an answer — “he went that way” — so it is an assertion made with an arm instead of a voice. A statement can be oral, written, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended it as an assertion. All four hearsay dangers apply to the pointing bystander just as they would to a speaking one.
✗ Not quite. The bystander meant the point as an answer — “he went that way” — an assertion made with an arm instead of a voice. The rule covers oral assertions, written assertions, and nonverbal conduct intended as an assertion. What the rule leaves out is conduct not intended to assert anything: a person running from a building, or opening an umbrella, communicates nothing on purpose, so it is not a statement.

Two quick boundaries follow from the word “person.” A machine readout — a radar display, a timestamp, a lab instrument's printout — is not a statement, because a machine is not a person; you attack it through calibration and reliability, not hearsay. An animal's bark or alert is not a statement either. And conduct nobody intended as communication (flinching, fleeing, opening an umbrella) asserts nothing, so it falls outside the rule.

Part two — “out of court” means out of this testimony

On the stand · the same witness

“The day after the crash, I told my sister the light was green for the truck.”

— Dana, testifying at trial, repeating her own earlier remark to prove the light was green.

Dana is right here, under oath, subject to cross-examination. Is her remark to her sister an out-of-court statement?

✓ Correct. The rule asks where the statement was made, not where the declarant is now. Dana's remark to her sister was not made while testifying at this trial, so it is out of court — and repeating it for its truth is hearsay unless a rule opens a door. When Dana spoke to her sister there was no oath, no jury watching, and no cross-examination; her presence today does not reach back and fix that.
✗ Not quite — and this is the single most common mistake. The rule asks where the statement was made, not where the declarant is now. Dana's remark to her sister was not made while testifying at this trial, so it is out of court, and repeating it for its truth is hearsay unless a rule opens a door. When Dana spoke to her sister there was no oath, no jury, and no cross-examination; her presence today does not reach back and fix that. (Rule 801(d)(1) opens doors for a few specific prior statements — §4 covers them.)

Part three — offered to prove what?

One statement, two lawsuits

“The brakes on that van have been shot for months.”

— a mechanic, to the van's owner, three weeks before the van hit a pedestrian.

The same sentence is offered twice. Which offer is hearsay?

✓ Correct. Offered to prove the brakes were actually bad, the statement's value depends on the mechanic being right — his perception, memory, narration, and sincerity all matter, and none of them can be tested. That is hearsay. Offered only to prove the owner heard a warning, the statement matters because it was said in the owner's presence, true or not — the mechanic could have been dead wrong and the owner would still be on notice. That use is not hearsay.
✗ The other one. Offered to prove the owner knew of the danger, the statement matters because it was said in the owner's presence — true or not. The mechanic could have been dead wrong about the brakes, and the owner would still have been warned. Nothing about that use depends on the mechanic's accuracy, so there is nothing cross-examination would need to test. Offered to prove the brakes were actually bad, though, everything depends on the mechanic being right — that use is hearsay.
FRE 801(a)–(c)

The Definition

FRE 801 ↗

You have now met every working part. Here is the sentence they add up to.

The rule, verbatim

(a) Statement. “Statement” means a person's oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended it as an assertion.

(b) Declarant. “Declarant” means the person who made the statement.

(c) Hearsay. “Hearsay” means a statement that:
(1) the declarant does not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing; and
(2) a party offers in evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement.

The opening ruling, resolved

“Maria told me the delivery truck ran the red light.”

Out-of-court statement by a person — 801(c)(1) is satisfied. Everything now rides on 801(c)(2): offered to prove the truck ran the light, it is hearsay and stays out unless a door opens. Offered to prove Maria was conscious and able to speak after the crash, it is not hearsay at all. Your first instinct as a judge should now be a question: “Counsel, what is this offered to prove?”

The method you will use on every question

Every hearsay problem in this lesson — and on your exam — runs through the same sequence of questions, in order. Steps 1 and 2 are the definition you just built. Steps 3 through 5 are the doors: categories of statements the rules admit anyway, which the next four sections teach. Steps 6 and 7 handle statements-inside-statements and criminal cases.

Two habits now, before the doors: always ask the steps in order (a purpose analysis at step 2 can end the problem before any exception matters), and at step 2, always ask “offered to prove what?” out loud. Press Watch to see the method run on the Maria statement.

The hearsay funnel

1Statement by a person, made out of court?No → not hearsay
2Offered to prove the truth of what it asserts?No → not hearsay; admissible for the other purpose
3801(d) exclusion — prior statement or opposing party?Yes → “not hearsay,” admitted
4803 exception? (availability doesn't matter)Yes → admitted
5Declarant unavailable + an 804 exception?Yes → admitted · No door at all → excluded (Rule 802)
6More than one layer? Run each layer separately (805)
7Criminal case, offered against the accused? Confrontation Clause (Crawford)

Press Watch to trace the Maria statement through the steps.

Practice · §2

Rule on each objection. Wrong options explain themselves, and you can retry.

Next · Offered for what purpose ↓

§3 · Offered for what purpose

The uses that are never hearsay at all

Step 2 of the funnel does more work than any exception. When a statement is offered for a purpose other than its truth, the hearsay dangers never arise — nobody is asking the jury to believe the declarant — so the rule simply does not apply. Three purposes account for most of these rulings, and exam questions reuse them constantly. One more scenario first:

On the stand · Jones v. Pratt (slander)

“I heard Pratt tell the whole tavern, ‘Jones picks pockets.’”

— a witness called by Jones, the plaintiff, to prove Pratt said it.

Pratt objects: hearsay. Your ruling?

✗ Overruled, actually. Ask the step-2 question: offered to prove what? Jones is not trying to prove he picks pockets — the opposite. He offers the words to prove the words were said, because saying them is the tort itself. When the words carry legal consequences just by being uttered — defamation, the “I accept” that forms a contract, the “this is yours” that makes a gift — lawyers call them verbal acts. Their truth is irrelevant, so they are not hearsay.
✓ Overruled. Jones is not trying to prove he picks pockets — the opposite. He offers the words to prove the words were said, because saying them is the tort itself. When words carry legal consequences just by being uttered — defamation, the “I accept” that forms a contract, the “this is yours” that makes a gift — lawyers call them verbal acts. Their truth is irrelevant, so they are not hearsay.
Purpose 1

Verbal Acts

The words themselves have legal significance — saying them is the act.

“I accept your offer.” · “This watch is now yours.” · “Jones picks pockets.”

Contract formation, gift, slander. The case turns on whether the words were spoken, not whether they were accurate. The tell: substituting a true version of the sentence wouldn't matter — the legal effect flows from the utterance.

Purpose 2

Effect on the Listener

Offered to prove what the hearer knew, feared, or was warned of — true or not.

“The brakes on that van have been shot for months.”

Offered to prove the owner was on notice of a danger. The mechanic could be wrong and the owner is still warned. Also covers threats offered to prove fear or duress, and information offered to explain why someone acted (why the officer went to the warehouse).

Purpose 3

Circumstantial State of Mind

The fact the declarant said it reveals their mental state — no one asks whether it's true.

“I am the Emperor of Japan.”

Offered in a competency dispute to show an irrational mind. Nobody offers it to prove he rules Japan — its falsity is the point. Keep this separate from Rule 803(3) in §5, which handles statements offered to prove the declarant's state of mind is as stated (“I hate Frank,” offered to prove hatred).

One procedural note that examiners reward: a statement admitted for a not-for-truth purpose comes in with a limiting instruction on request (Rule 105) — the judge tells the jury it may consider the statement for the permitted purpose only. On an essay, say which purpose, and say the instruction limits the use.

Practice · §3

Same bench, harder calls. Watch for step 2 ending the analysis before any exception is needed.

Next · The 801(d) exclusions ↓

§4 · The 801(d) exclusions

Statements the rules label “not hearsay”

The next two categories meet the full definition — out-of-court statements offered for their truth — but Rule 801(d) declares them “not hearsay” anyway. The label is a drafting choice, and it is worth keeping straight for exams: 801(d) statements are excluded from the definition, while the §5 and §6 categories are exceptions to the ban. Same practical result — the evidence comes in for its truth — different vocabulary, and different requirements.

On the stand · the recanting eyewitness

“I told the grand jury I saw Avery go into the pawnshop. Today I'm telling you: the man I saw was a stranger.”

— the State's own eyewitness, under oath, subject to cross. The prosecutor offers the grand-jury version to prove Avery went in.

Under the §2 definition, the grand-jury statement is out of court and offered for its truth. Does it stay out?

✗ It comes in. Think about which dangers survive here. The declarant is on the stand, under oath, and the defense can cross-examine her about both versions right now — the jury watches her explain herself. The earlier statement was itself given under oath before a grand jury. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) admits a prior inconsistent statement as substantive evidence when the declarant testifies, is subject to cross about it, and gave the earlier statement under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition.
✓ There is. The declarant is on the stand, under oath, and the defense can cross-examine her about both versions right now — the jury watches her explain herself. The earlier statement was itself given under oath before a grand jury. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) admits a prior inconsistent statement as substantive evidence when the declarant testifies, is subject to cross about it, and gave the earlier statement under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition.
FRE 801(d)(1)

A Declarant-Witness's Prior Statement

FRE 801(d)(1) ↗

The declarant is here and crossable — the missing testing the rule worries about is available after all.

The rule, verbatim

The declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination about a prior statement, and the statement:

(A) is inconsistent with the declarant's testimony and was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, or other proceeding or in a deposition;

(B) is consistent with the declarant's testimony and is offered: [abridged — full text below]

(C) identifies a person as someone the declarant perceived earlier.

Full text of (B)

(B) is consistent with the declarant's testimony and is offered:
(i) to rebut an express or implied charge that the declarant recently fabricated it or acted from a recent improper influence or motive in so testifying; or
(ii) to rehabilitate the declarant's credibility as a witness when attacked on another ground; or

What to watch on exams

(A) needs the oath-and-proceeding pedigree: a grand jury or deposition qualifies; an unsworn police interview does not — that one impeaches credibility but cannot prove the fact. (B) only fires after the witness's credibility is attacked. (C) is broader than it looks: an earlier lineup or photo identification comes in substantively even if the witness's memory has since failed, as long as the witness testifies and is subject to cross.

Recorded at the scene · State v. Boone

“I never miss. I clipped that guy from three hundred yards.”

— the defendant, boasting to a friend a week after the shooting. The prosecution offers it.

Boone's lawyer objects: hearsay — an out-of-court statement offered to prove Boone fired the shot. Your ruling?

✗ Overruled. This is an opposing party's statement — Rule 801(d)(2)(A) — and it needs no exception, no reliability, and no showing that it was against Boone's interest when he said it. The rationale isn't trust; it's the adversary system: a party cannot complain that he had no chance to cross-examine himself. He can take the stand and explain the boast. Anything a party ever said, offered against that party, clears the hearsay bar.
✓ Overruled. An opposing party's statement — Rule 801(d)(2)(A) — needs no exception, no reliability, and no showing that it was against Boone's interest when he said it. The rationale isn't trust; it's the adversary system: a party cannot complain that he had no chance to cross-examine himself. He can take the stand and explain the boast. Anything a party ever said, offered against that party, clears the hearsay bar.
FRE 801(d)(2)

An Opposing Party's Statement

FRE 801(d)(2) ↗

What you said can be used against you — and so can what your agents and co-conspirators said for you.

Purpose

This door rests on fairness, not reliability. The hearsay rule protects a party's chance to test the declarant — but when the declarant is the party, there is nothing to protect: you cannot be denied the chance to cross-examine yourself, and you are free to take the stand and explain. The rule then extends that logic to statements the party adopted, authorized, or made through agents and co-conspirators.

The rule, verbatim

The statement is offered against an opposing party and:

(A) was made by the party in an individual or representative capacity;

(B) is one the party manifested that it adopted or believed to be true;

(C) was made by a person whom the party authorized to make a statement on the subject;

(D) was made by the party's agent or employee on a matter within the scope of that relationship and while it existed; or

(E) was made by the party's coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy.

Full text — the foundation sentences

The statement must be considered but does not by itself establish the declarant's authority under (C); the existence or scope of the relationship under (D); or the existence of the conspiracy or participation in it under (E).

If a party's claim, defense, or potential liability is directly derived from a declarant or the declarant's principal, a statement that would be admissible against the declarant or the principal under this rule is also admissible against the party.

What to watch on exams

No personal knowledge required; no against-interest requirement; opinions count. (B) adoption can be by conduct or by silence, when a reasonable person would have denied the accusation. (D) asks whether the topic was within the employee's job, not whether the employer authorized the confession. (E) has two requirements that decide exam questions: the statement must come during the conspiracy (not after arrest ends it) and in furtherance of it (recruiting, planning, reassuring — not confessing or boasting afterward).

Practice · §4

The wrong options here are the neighboring doors — the point is saying why the neighbor fails.

Next · The 803 exceptions ↓

§5 · The 803 exceptions

Statements trusted for how they were made

Rule 803 lists twenty-three exceptions that apply “regardless of whether the declarant is available as a witness.” Each one describes a situation where the circumstances of the statement do some of the work cross-examination would have done. Courses and exams concentrate on seven of them, and so does this section. Start with the pair that students confuse most:

Two bystanders, one crash

Bystander one, watching it happen, in an even voice: “That van is drifting across the center line.” Bystander two, ten minutes later, still shaking: “That van never even braked!”

Neither can be found by trial. Both statements are offered to prove how the van was driven.

Which statement comes in?

± Half right. The calm one comes in — but so does the other. Bystander one spoke while perceiving the event: no gap between seeing and saying means no time to misremember or fabricate. That is the present sense impression, 803(1). Bystander two spoke under the continuing stress of a startling event: the theory is that excitement suspends the capacity to fabricate. That is the excited utterance, 803(2). Two different substitutes for cross-examination — a clock, and a state of mind.
± Half right. The shaken one comes in — but so does the other. Bystander two spoke under the continuing stress of a startling event: the theory is that excitement suspends the capacity to fabricate. That is the excited utterance, 803(2). Bystander one spoke while perceiving the event: no gap between seeing and saying means no time to misremember or fabricate. That is the present sense impression, 803(1). Two different substitutes for cross-examination — a clock, and a state of mind.
✓ Both. Bystander one spoke while perceiving the event: no gap between seeing and saying means no time to misremember or fabricate — the present sense impression, 803(1). Bystander two spoke under the continuing stress of a startling event: the theory is that excitement suspends the capacity to fabricate — the excited utterance, 803(2). Two different substitutes for cross-examination: a clock, and a state of mind.
FRE 803(1)

Present Sense Impression

FRE 803(1) ↗

Said while it happened — no gap for memory or invention to work in.

The rule, verbatim

A statement describing or explaining an event or condition, made while or immediately after the declarant perceived it.

What to watch

The clock is strict: “while or immediately after” means seconds to a very few minutes. The subject is narrow: the statement must describe or explain the event itself. No startle required; a calm narrator qualifies.

FRE 803(2)

Excited Utterance

FRE 803(2) ↗

Said under stress of a startling event — excitement leaves no room to fabricate.

The rule, verbatim

A statement relating to a startling event or condition, made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement that it caused.

What to watch

The clock is loose: minutes, sometimes longer, as long as the stress genuinely continues — look for facts like sobbing, shaking, screaming. The subject is broader: merely relating to the startling event. Both requirements are about the moment of speaking: startling event, and still under its stress.

The discrimination, compressed: 803(1) runs on a clock, 803(2) runs on stress. A calm statement made during the event fits (1) but not (2); an agitated statement made ten minutes later fits (2) but not (1); the next morning, calm, it fits neither and stays out unless another door opens.

FRE 803(3)

Then-Existing State of Mind or Condition

FRE 803(3) ↗

People report their own current feelings, plans, and pains more reliably than they report the outside world.

Purpose

Two of the four dangers nearly vanish here: a declarant cannot easily misperceive or misremember what she herself feels or intends at the moment she speaks. Sincerity remains a risk — so the rule draws a hard line at statements that look backward at facts in the world.

The rule, verbatim

A statement of the declarant's then-existing state of mind (such as motive, intent, or plan) or emotional, sensory, or physical condition (such as mental feeling, pain, or bodily health), but not including a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed unless it relates to the validity or terms of the declarant's will.

Worked examples — the line the carve-out draws

“I'm meeting Angelo at the marina tomorrow night.”

A statement of present intent — admissible under 803(3), and under the classic Hillmon doctrine the jury may infer she followed through and went. Forward-looking, first-person: fine.

“I remember Paul following me home last Tuesday.”

A statement of memory, offered to prove the thing remembered — exactly what the carve-out forbids. Backward-looking statements would swallow the whole hearsay rule if they came in as “state of mind,” because every assertion about the world can be rephrased as “I believe X.” The lone exception: statements about the declarant's own will.

FRE 803(4)

Statement Made for Medical Diagnosis or Treatment

FRE 803(4) ↗

Patients have a life-and-limb incentive to tell medical staff the truth.

The rule, verbatim

A statement that:
(A) is made for — and is reasonably pertinent to — medical diagnosis or treatment; and
(B) describes medical history; past or present symptoms or sensations; their inception; or their general cause.

What to watch

“A car hit me in the crosswalk, and my hip has hurt ever since.”

Cause and symptoms — pertinent, admissible, even though it reaches back in time (a deliberate contrast with 803(3)'s carve-out: the treatment incentive substitutes). But “the driver ran a red light” would stay out: fault is not pertinent to treatment. The audience can be any medical personnel — triage nurse, EMT, or a physician hired only to diagnose for litigation.

FRE 803(5)

Recorded Recollection

FRE 803(5) ↗

The witness's memory is gone, but a record made while it was fresh survives.

The rule, verbatim

A record that:
(A) is on a matter the witness once knew about but now cannot recall well enough to testify fully and accurately;
(B) was made or adopted by the witness when the matter was fresh in the witness's memory; and
(C) accurately reflects the witness's knowledge.
If admitted, the record may be read into evidence but may be received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party.

What to watch

The witness must actually be on the stand and out of memory — try refreshing recollection first (showing the note under Rule 612 is not hearsay at all, since the testimony, not the note, is the evidence). And note the last sentence: the proponent reads the record aloud; only the adversary can make it an exhibit the jury takes to deliberations.

FRE 803(6)

Business Records

FRE 803(6) ↗

Routine records made because the business runs on them — accuracy is a job requirement.

The rule, verbatim (abridged)

A record of an act, event, condition, opinion, or diagnosis if:
(A) the record was made at or near the time by — or from information transmitted by — someone with knowledge;
(B) the record was kept in the course of a regularly conducted activity of a business, organization, occupation, or calling, whether or not for profit;
(C) making the record was a regular practice of that activity; [(D)–(E) below]

Full text of (D)–(E)

(D) all these conditions are shown by the testimony of the custodian or another qualified witness, or by a certification that complies with Rule 902(11) or (12) or with a statute permitting certification; and
(E) the opponent does not show that the source of information or the method or circumstances of preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness.

What to watch

Everyone in the chain must act in the business routine: a driver's log entry qualifies; a customer's statement written into the log is a second layer needing its own door (§7). And a report prepared for litigation fails — the railroad's post-accident report in Palmer v. Hoffman was held outside the regular course of railroading, and under today's rule its litigation origin also triggers (E)'s trustworthiness bar.

FRE 803(8)

Public Records

FRE 803(8) ↗

Public officers record under legal duty — but the rule refuses to let police reports convict.

The rule, verbatim

A record or statement of a public office if:
(A) it sets out:
(i) the office's activities;
(ii) a matter observed while under a legal duty to report, but not including, in a criminal case, a matter observed by law-enforcement personnel; or
(iii) in a civil case or against the government in a criminal case, factual findings from a legally authorized investigation; and
(B) the opponent does not show that the source of information or other circumstances indicate a lack of trustworthiness.

What to watch

The two marked limits are the exam. A police officer's observation report cannot be offered against a criminal defendant under (ii) — and courts refuse to let the prosecution smuggle the same report in as a “business record” under 803(6). Investigative findings under (iii) flow one way in criminal cases: against the government only.

Practice · §5

Seven rulings. The distractors are the neighboring exceptions — say why the neighbor fails.

Next · The 804 exceptions ↓

§6 · The 804 exceptions

Exceptions that require an unavailable declarant

The 803 exceptions never ask where the declarant is. The 804 family does, and the reason is worth stating: these statements are second-best evidence. Former testimony is worse than live testimony; a statement against interest is worse than the declarant on the stand. The rule accepts second-best only when best is impossible — so every 804 analysis has two steps: prove unavailability under 804(a), then fit an exception under 804(b).

FRE 804(a)

Criteria for Being Unavailable

FRE 804(a) ↗

Unavailable means the testimony cannot be had — the declarant's body in the courthouse is not the question.

The rule, verbatim (abridged)

A declarant is considered to be unavailable as a witness if the declarant:
(1) is exempted from testifying about the subject matter of the declarant's statement because the court rules that a privilege applies;
(2) refuses to testify about the subject matter despite a court order to do so;
(3) testifies to not remembering the subject matter;
(4) cannot be present or testify at the trial or hearing because of death or a then-existing infirmity, physical illness, or mental illness; or
(5) is absent from the trial or hearing and the statement's proponent has not been able, by process or other reasonable means, to procure the declarant's attendance [or attendance/testimony, depending on the exception — full text below]

Full text of (5) and the wrongdoing sentence

(5) is absent from the trial or hearing and the statement's proponent has not been able, by process or other reasonable means, to procure:
(A) the declarant's attendance, in the case of a hearsay exception under Rule 804(b)(1) or (6); or
(B) the declarant's attendance or testimony, in the case of a hearsay exception under Rule 804(b)(2), (3), or (4).

But this subdivision (a) does not apply if the statement's proponent procured or wrongfully caused the declarant's unavailability as a witness in order to prevent the declarant from attending or testifying.

What to watch

A declarant sitting in the front row is still unavailable if a court upholds her privilege claim, she defies an order to testify, or she genuinely cannot remember. And the last sentence cuts off gamesmanship: a proponent who caused the unavailability to keep the declarant off the stand cannot use it.

In the ambulance · State v. Ray

“I'm not going to make it. Tell them Ray did this.”

— the stabbing victim to a paramedic. She survives — barely — and is in a coma at the time of Ray's attempted-murder trial.

The victim never died. Can the statement come in as a dying declaration?

✗ It can come in. Read the rule's actual triggers: the declarant must be unavailable (a coma qualifies under 804(a)(4)), and the statement must have been made while believing death to be imminent, about its cause or circumstances. Belief at the moment of speaking is what matters — actual death never appears in the rule. What does limit the rule is the forum: prosecutions for homicide, and civil cases. An attempted-murder prosecution is neither, so here the statement needs a different door (excited utterance is the natural one).
✓ Right — belief, not death, is the trigger. The declarant must be unavailable (a coma qualifies under 804(a)(4)), and the statement must have been made while believing death to be imminent, about its cause or circumstances. Actual death never appears in the rule. But check the forum before you rest: the exception applies only in prosecutions for homicide and in civil cases. An attempted-murder prosecution is neither — so here the statement needs a different door (excited utterance is the natural one).
FRE 804(b)(1)

Former Testimony

FRE 804(b)(1) ↗

The testing already happened — oath, transcript, and a party with the same motive to cross-examine.

The rule, verbatim

Testimony that:
(A) was given as a witness at a trial, hearing, or lawful deposition, whether given during the current proceeding or a different one; and
(B) is now offered against a party who had — or, in a civil case, whose predecessor in interest had — an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross-, or redirect examination.

What to watch

The question is never “was there a transcript?” — it is whether the party you now offer it against already had a fair shot at this witness, with a similar motive. A preliminary-hearing cross by the same defendant usually qualifies; testimony from an unrelated case against a different party does not.

FRE 804(b)(2)

Dying Declaration

FRE 804(b)(2) ↗

The theory: a person who believes death is imminent has no reason to lie.

The rule, verbatim

In a prosecution for homicide or in a civil case, a statement that the declarant, while believing the declarant's death to be imminent, made about its cause or circumstances.

What to watch

Four elements, each tested: the forum (homicide or civil — not robbery, not attempted murder); belief of imminent death when speaking; subject limited to the death's cause or circumstances; and unavailability — which belief satisfies only if the declarant is in fact unavailable at trial. Death is sufficient but not required.

FRE 804(b)(3)

Statement Against Interest

FRE 804(b)(3) ↗

People do not confess to crimes or debts they don't have — self-harm is the guarantee of sincerity.

Purpose

This exception and Rule 801(d)(2) are the pair students mix up most, because both involve statements that hurt the speaker. Keep the two apart by asking who the declarant is. 801(d)(2) needs a party — and needs nothing else: any statement, harmful or boastful, offered against them. 804(b)(3) works for anyone's statement — a bystander, a missing friend — but demands the two things the party rule never asks for: the statement must have been against the declarant's interest when made, and the declarant must be unavailable.

The rule, verbatim

A statement that:
(A) a reasonable person in the declarant's position would have made only if the person believed it to be true because, when made, it was so contrary to the declarant's proprietary or pecuniary interest or had so great a tendency to invalidate the declarant's claim against someone else or to expose the declarant to civil or criminal liability; and
(B) if offered in a criminal case as one that tends to expose the declarant to criminal liability, is supported by corroborating circumstances that clearly indicate its trustworthiness after considering the totality of circumstances under which it was made and any evidence that supports or undermines it.

What to watch

Measure “against interest” at the moment of speaking, sentence by sentence — a statement that shifts blame to someone else (“Joe planned it, I just drove”) is self-serving in part, and courts admit only the genuinely disserving parts. In criminal cases, statements exposing the declarant to criminal liability need corroboration under (B).

FRE 804(b)(6)

Forfeiture by Wrongdoing

FRE 804(b)(6) ↗

A party who wrongfully causes the declarant's absence loses the objection to it.

The rule, verbatim

A statement offered against a party that wrongfully caused — or acquiesced in wrongfully causing — the declarant's unavailability as a witness, and did so intending that result.

What to watch

The intent element decides exam questions: the wrongdoing must have been done to prevent the testimony. A defendant who murders the declarant for unrelated reasons has not forfeited under this rule (the Supreme Court held exactly that for the parallel constitutional doctrine in Giles v. California). When it applies, it forfeits the hearsay objection — and, as §7 explains, the Confrontation Clause objection too.

Practice · §6

Two-step discipline: name the 804(a) ground first, then the (b) exception.

§7 · Layers and confrontation

Hearsay within hearsay

Real evidence rarely arrives one statement at a time. A hospital record contains a nurse's note, which quotes the patient. Each quoted layer is its own out-of-court statement, and Rule 805 states the discipline in one sentence:

Hearsay within hearsay is not excluded by the rule against hearsay if each part of the combined statements conforms with an exception to the rule. — Fed. R. Evid. 805 (source ↗). Courts read “exception” to include the 801(d) exclusions — any door works, but every layer needs one.

Worked example

Two Layers, Two Doors

The ER record: “Patient states: ‘My husband pushed me down the stairs.’” Offered to prove the push.

Layer one — the record itself. Made at or near the time, by staff with knowledge, in the hospital's regular practice: Rule 803(6), business record.

Layer two — the patient's sentence inside it. The business-records door does not cover her — she is not part of the hospital's routine. Her statement needs its own door: made for treatment and describing the cause of her injury, it fits Rule 803(4) (courts admit the abuser's identity in domestic-violence cases where it is pertinent to treatment and safety).

Both doors open, so the whole package is admissible. If either layer had no door — say the note recorded a bystander's remark to the nurse — that layer would fail and the package stays out.

The Confrontation Clause — the constitutional overlay

Everything so far has been the Federal Rules. In a criminal case, one more authority gets a vote, and it outranks all of them. Raleigh's demand from §1 became constitutional text:

“In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right … to be confronted with the witnesses against him …” — U.S. Const. amend. VI (source ↗)

Two statements, one victim · State v. Cole

Statement one: a 911 call, screaming, while the assault is still happening — “He's here, he's got my keys, help me!” Statement two: an hour later at the station, calm, a signed narrative describing the attack.

The victim does not testify at trial. The prosecution offers both statements.

Assume both statements clear a hearsay exception. Does the Confrontation Clause treat them the same?

✗ It splits them. The audience is not the test — the primary purpose is. In Davis v. Washington, the Supreme Court held a 911 call made to get help during an ongoing emergency is nontestimonial: the caller is crying for rescue, not building a case. The calm stationhouse narrative is testimonial — its primary purpose is to establish past facts for prosecution, which makes the declarant a “witness” the accused is entitled to confront. Statement one comes in; statement two is barred unless she testifies, or is unavailable and was previously cross-examined.
✓ It splits them. The audience is not the test — the primary purpose is. In Davis v. Washington, the Supreme Court held a 911 call made to get help during an ongoing emergency is nontestimonial: the caller is crying for rescue, not building a case. The calm stationhouse narrative is testimonial — its primary purpose is to establish past facts for prosecution, which makes the declarant a “witness” the accused is entitled to confront. Statement one comes in; statement two is barred unless she testifies, or is unavailable and was previously cross-examined.
U.S. Const. amend. VI · Crawford v. Washington (2004)

The Testimonial Framework

Crawford ↗

Testimonial statements of an absent declarant are barred unless she is unavailable and was already cross-examined.

Purpose

Crawford reset the field in 2004, citing Raleigh's trial as the abuse the Clause was written against: the government proving its case with accusations produced by official questioning, never tested in front of the accused. So the Clause targets statements that function like testimony — and leaves the rest to the ordinary hearsay rules.

The analysis, in order

1. Criminal case, statement offered against the accused? If not, the Clause never applies — civil cases run on the hearsay rules alone.
2. Is the statement testimonial? Ask its primary purpose. Testimonial: stationhouse interrogations about past events, affidavits, sworn statements, forensic certificates prepared for trial. Nontestimonial: statements to meet an ongoing emergency (Davis, and the shot victim in Michigan v. Bryant), casual remarks to friends, most statements to non-police (a child's report to a teacher in Ohio v. Clark).
3. Does the declarant testify at trial? Confrontation satisfied.
4. If not: the testimonial statement is admissible only if the declarant is unavailable and the accused had a prior opportunity to cross-examine — and forfeiture by wrongdoing extinguishes the objection entirely.

What to watch

A statement can clear a hearsay exception and still be barred by the Clause — the two screens are independent, and an exam answer must run both. Crawford also noted the historic pedigree of dying declarations, which courts have treated as surviving even when testimonial.

The whole method, once more

You now own every step. Press Watch to see the funnel run on a full exam-style package — a police report quoting an excited bystander, offered in a criminal trial — and notice how the analysis can die at a different step for each layer.

Then prove you have the order: rebuild the funnel from shuffled steps. Order matters — a purpose ruling at step 2 moots every exception, and the constitutional check waits until a statement has already survived the rules.

The morning docket

Ten objections, mixed across everything you have learned, in no helpful order — the way they arrive in a courtroom and on an exam. Each row checks itself off when you complete the work it names — drills check off on a correct answer (retries count), the docket on answering all ten.

Checklist complete. You can define hearsay, catch not-for-truth purposes, route statements through 801(d), 803, and 804, dismantle layered packages, and run the Confrontation Clause — every step of the federal analysis this lesson covers.

What this lesson does not teach

  • Rules 806 and 807. Attacking an absent declarant's credibility, and the residual exception for trustworthy statements that fit no category, are real but rarely course-central.
  • Impeachment mechanics. Prior inconsistent statements used only to impeach travel under Rule 613, with their own procedure.
  • Neighboring doctrines that share exam space: personal knowledge (602), authentication, Bruton problems with co-defendant confessions, and the judge-jury split on preliminary facts (104).
  • State law. This lesson is the federal rules; states vary — California's hearsay statute, for example, is organized differently and diverges on several exceptions. If your course uses state rules, your professor's materials govern.
  • This is exam preparation, not legal advice.

This week's transfer task

  • Take one fact pattern from your casebook or a released exam from your professor and write the full funnel analysis — every layer, every step, a “because” sentence at each ruling.
  • In your next case reading, when an opinion quotes an out-of-court statement, name the door it came through before the court tells you.

Quick Reference

The definition · 801(a)–(c)

HearsayAn out-of-court statement (a person's intended assertion — oral, written, or conduct) offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted. Machines and animals are not declarants.
Not for truthVerbal acts (words with legal effect) · effect on the listener (notice, fear, why someone acted) · circumstantial evidence of state of mind. Limiting instruction on request (Rule 105).

Exclusions · 801(d)

801(d)(1) Prior statementsDeclarant testifies + subject to cross. (A) inconsistent — needs oath at a proceeding/deposition. (B) consistent — to rebut fabrication charges or rehabilitate. (C) identification of a person.
801(d)(2) Opposing partyOffered against a party: their own statement, adopted, authorized, agent/employee within scope during employment, or coconspirator during + in furtherance. No against-interest or knowledge requirement.

Exceptions — availability immaterial · 803

803(1) Present sense impressionDescribes/explains an event, made while or immediately after perceiving it. Strict clock, no startle needed.
803(2) Excited utteranceRelates to a startling event, made under its continuing stress. Loose clock, stress required.
803(3) State of mindThen-existing state of mind, emotion, or physical condition; intent can prove later conduct (Hillmon). Never memory/belief to prove the fact remembered (except wills).
803(4) MedicalMade for and pertinent to diagnosis or treatment: history, symptoms, general cause. Fault stays out; any medical personnel counts.
803(5) Recorded recollectionWitness once knew, now can't recall; record made/adopted while fresh; accurate. Read aloud; exhibit only if the adversary offers it.
803(6) Business recordsMade at/near the time, by/from someone with knowledge, regular activity + regular practice, custodian foundation, and no trustworthiness problem (litigation-driven reports fail).
803(8) Public recordsOffice activities; matters observed under legal duty — but not police observations in criminal cases; investigative findings in civil cases or against the government. No 803(6) end-run.

Exceptions — unavailability required · 804

804(a) UnavailablePrivilege, refusal despite order, memory failure, death/illness, or absence beyond reasonable means — unless the proponent caused it.
804(b)(1) Former testimonyPrior trial/hearing/deposition testimony, offered against a party who had opportunity + similar motive to develop it (civil: predecessor in interest).
804(b)(2) Dying declarationHomicide prosecutions or civil cases; belief of imminent death; about its cause/circumstances. Death not required — unavailability is.
804(b)(3) Against interestAnyone's statement so contrary to their own interest a reasonable person wouldn't say it falsely; measured when made; criminal-liability statements need corroboration.
804(b)(6) ForfeitureParty wrongfully caused (or acquiesced in causing) the declarant's unavailability, intending to prevent testimony. Forfeits Confrontation objections too.

Layers and the constitution

805 Hearsay within hearsayEvery layer needs its own door — exclusions count. One doorless layer sinks the package.
Crawford frameworkCriminal case, against the accused, testimonial statement (primary purpose = proving past facts for prosecution): barred unless declarant testifies, or is unavailable + was previously cross-examined. Emergencies (Davis/Bryant) and most non-police audiences (Clark) are nontestimonial.
